answer:
Domain adaptation addresses differences between a labeled source distribution and a target distribution, such as clean studio images versus blurry mobile images. DANN trains a shared encoder with a task head and a source/target discriminator. The domain head minimizes domain classification loss, while a gradient-reversal layer multiplies its encoder gradient by $-\lambda$, encouraging features that hide domain identity while preserving source-task prediction. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.07818)

Marginal feature alignment is useful only when compatible with the task: different label proportions or class-conditional shifts can make indiscriminate alignment harmful. Evaluate labeled target data when available, target-specific augmentations, subgroup performance, and calibration. Avoid using a final target test set for tuning. Domain-confused features are not proof of semantic alignment or target accuracy, especially when the simulator omits important real-world factors.
